t: Maximum XOR With an Element From Array — Binary Trie Meets Offline Queries
o: You are given up to $10^5$ numbers and up to $10^5$ queries; query $i$ hands you a value $x_i$ and a cap $m_i$, and asks for the largest XOR between $x_i$ and any array element that does not exceed $m_i$ (or **-1** if every element exceeds the cap). In Example 1, `nums = [0,1,2,3,4]`: query `[3,1]` may only use 0 and 1, and 0 XOR 3 = 3 beats 1 XOR 3 = 2, so the answer is 3; query `[1,3]` may use 0..3 and 1 XOR 2 = 3 wins; query `[5,6]` may use everything and 5 XOR 2 = 7 is the maximum. In Example 2, `[12,4]` finds 12 XOR 3 = 15, while `[8,1]` has no eligible element at all and yields -1. Answering each query by scanning the array costs about $10^{10}$ operations — far too slow. Since maximizing XOR is a greedy bit-by-bit decision and every value fits in 30 bits ($\le 10^9 < 2^{30}$), a binary trie can resolve each query in $O(30)$ — provided we can control which elements are currently eligible, which sorting both arrays by their thresholds enables.
k: Maximizing x XOR y is greedy: walking from the highest bit, prefer the branch holding the opposite bit of x; a binary trie turns that walk into O(30).
Eligibility only depends on elements being at most m_i, so sorting queries by m_i and inserting numbers incrementally avoids rebuilding any structure per query.
Values are below $2^{30}$, so 30 levels of bits suffice for the trie.

a.n: Approach 1: Answer Each Query by Scanning
a.i: For every query, look at every number whose value is at most the cap and track the best XOR seen. This directly mirrors the problem statement and is a perfect baseline to reason about before optimizing. With both dimensions at $10^5$ it performs up to $10^{10}$ operations, so it exceeds the time limit on real inputs.
s: For each query (x, m), initialize the best value to -1.
Iterate over all nums; for every element v <= m, update best with max(best, v XOR x).
Append best (still -1 if nothing qualified) to the answer list.
a.t: O(n · q) — every query scans all n numbers
a.sp: O(1) — only the output list is allocated

a.n: Approach 2: Sort Queries and Walk a Binary Trie
a.i: Store eligible numbers in a binary trie keyed by their 30 bits. To respect the cap, process queries in increasing m order while sweeping nums in increasing value order: before answering a query, insert every number that just became eligible. Each answer is then a single root-to-leaf descent that greedily prefers the opposite bit of x wherever possible; taking an opposite bit always dominates any combination of lower bits, so the first feasible choice at each level is optimal. This offline reordering is what makes one trie serve all queries.
s: Sort nums ascending; sort queries by cap m, remembering original indices.
Walk queries in cap order, inserting into a 30-level binary trie every num that has become eligible (num <= m).
If no number was eligible yet, leave -1 for that query.
Otherwise descend from the top bit, taking the child with the bit opposite to x's current bit whenever it exists and setting that result bit to 1.
Write each answer back to its original query position.
a.t: O(30 · (n + q) + n log n + q log q) — each number and query walks 30 trie levels; sorting nums and queries adds the logarithmic factors
a.sp: O(30 · n) — the trie holds at most one node per bit per inserted number

w: In an interview, present the brute force briefly, then move to the offline-sort-plus-trie solution — it is the intended answer and cleanly demonstrates bitwise greedy reasoning plus offline query processing. Common pitfalls: returning 0 instead of -1 when no element satisfies the cap; iterating bits from 30 instead of 29 (values reach 10^9 which still fits in 30 bits); forgetting to restore answers to original query order after sorting; and mishandling the sweep when several numbers share the same value. Edge cases: caps smaller than every element, duplicated values in nums (harmless — identical trie paths get re-inserted), and x = 0 (the answer is then just the largest eligible number). Likely follow-ups: forced online queries require a persistent trie keyed by insertion time; related variants include maximum XOR pair inside one array or maximum XOR subarray via prefix-XOR tries.
